subject: physics
question_text: Give the expression for the excess pressure in a soap bubble.

mark_split.label: A soap bubble has two surfaces

verification.note: Asked in TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, March 2016 (Q6) — Section A, 2 marks. The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: a soap bubble in air is a thin liquid film with air on both faces, so it has TWO liquid–air surfaces; each curved surface of radius r contributes an excess pressure 2T/r, giving ΔP = 4T/r. This is the reason the soap bubble differs from a liquid drop and from an air bubble inside a liquid, which each have ONE surface and ΔP = 2T/r.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: A soap bubble has two surfaces
lines: A soap bubble in air is a thin film of
soap solution with air inside it and air
So the film has TWO liquid surfaces: an
inner surface and an outer surface.
Each curved surface of radius r on its own
steps.margin_note: First mark. State that the film has two surfaces. This is what produces the 4.
steps.why: The number of liquid surfaces fixes the numerator of the formula. A soap film has air on both faces, so both faces are liquid surfaces under tension and both contribute.
common_mistakes: Writing 2T/r, which is the value for one surface only.
Saying a soap bubble has two surfaces because it has an inside and an outside radius. The two radii are almost equal; it is the two liquid faces that matter.

recall.must_convey: That a soap bubble is a film with air on both sides, so it has two liquid surfaces, each contributing 2T/r.
accept: air inside and air outside the film

steps.memory_tip: Air inside, air outside, so both faces of the film are liquid surfaces.

steps.label: ΔP = 4T/r
lines: ΔP is the pressure inside the bubble minus
the pressure outside, T is the surface
tension of the soap solution and r is the
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The 4 is the number being checked. Write r to the first power.
steps.why: The surface count multiplies the single-surface result, so the formula follows from the first step and does not have to be memorised on its own.
common_mistakes: Writing 4T/r² . The radius appears to the first power, not squared.
Calling ΔP the pressure inside the bubble. It is the difference between inside and outside.

recall.must_convey: That the excess pressure in a soap bubble is 4T by r, with T the surface tension and r the radius.

steps.memory_tip: Count surfaces, then multiply 2T/r by that count. Bubble: 2 × 2T/r = 4T/r.

insider_note: One mark is the surface count, one is the formula, so 2T/r for a bubble loses both. The 4 is all that separates this from the drop.
